paper.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

summary: By 1997 the web had too many pages to sort by hand, and keyword matching returned a lot of junk. This paper describes Google, a prototype search engine that ranks pages by who links to them (PageRank) and answers searches from a big word-to-pages index.

hook.teaser: How can a computer tell which web page is the best one, when it can't read minds?

blocks.deck: The web had millions of pages and no good way to sort them. Two students had an idea: a page matters if other pages point to it.

slides.label: Too many pages

media.alt: A huge pile of web pages with one tiny gold page buried inside. Below: So many pages, so few good ones.

slides.label: Links are votes
slides.caption: Fig. 2. When many pages point at one page, that page is probably worth a look.

blocks.kicker: Computer science / A picture story in four parts
blocks.title: How a search engine picks what to show

chapters.title: Too many pages, too few good ones
chapters.caption: Imagine a library where new books arrive every minute and nobody sorts the shelves. In 1997, search engines could find pages that held your words, but a lot of what they found was junk. People only look at the first few results, so the best pages had to come first.

media.alt: Messy shelves overflowing with pages. Below: shelves that nobody sorted.

chapters.title: A link is a vote
chapters.caption: When one page links to another, it is a little like a vote. A vote from a well-liked page counts for more, and a page that links to many pages splits its vote between them. The paper calls the score PageRank. Pages with votes from many places, or from a few important places, rise to the top.

media.alt: Arrows from several pages lead to one page. The arrow from the biggest page is the thickest. Below: big votes and small votes.

chapters.title: Walk, file, look up
chapters.caption: Think of a librarian. First she walks the web and brings back a copy of every page. Then she writes a giant index, like the one at the back of a book: for each word, which pages have it. When you search, she finds the pages that have all your words and ranks them by how well the words match and how high their PageRank is. The paper's names are crawler, repository and inverted index.

media.alt: Three boxes in a row joined by arrows: crawl, index, answer. Below: fetch it, file it, look it up.

chapters.title: A first test, with honest limits
chapters.caption: The authors searched for “bill clinton.” Many of their top results were pages from the White House's own site, and none were broken links. They say this is largely because those pages have a high PageRank. They are careful, though: they did not run a full study with users, so this is their own experience, not proof. They also report a working prototype with at least 24 million pages. See the paper's results section ↗

media.alt: A short list of search results with a bar beside each. Below: 24 million pages, one first test.

blocks.kicker: Computer science / Under the hood / A comic in five strips
blocks.title: How the search engine actually works
blocks.deck: Read each strip from left to right. We follow one search, from a web of links to a list of results.
blocks.howTo: The drawings are made up to explain the idea. Where a caption names a number or a part such as PageRank or inverted index, those are the paper's own. The paper's numbers are in the evidence box at the end.

strips.title: The web is a web of friends
strips.kicker: How pages link to each other
strips.grownUpWords: hyperlinks, backlinks and the citation (link) graph

panels.caption: Picture each web page as a kid at school. A page can point to another page with a link, like saying “go meet my friend.”

media.alt: Four kids standing apart, one pointing to another with an arrow.

panels.caption: When lots of kids point at the same kid, that kid is probably worth meeting. The authors treated links like citations in a science paper. They built maps with as many as 518 million links.

media.alt: Many arrows from small circles all pointing at one big circle.

panels.caption: But a pointing finger from a famous kid should count more than one from a kid nobody knows. Not every link is worth the same.

media.alt: One thick arrow from a big circle and one thin arrow from a small circle, both pointing at a page.

strips.title: A popularity vote that keeps updating
strips.grownUpWords: PageRank, damping factor and the random surfer

panels.caption: Every page hands out its score to the pages it links to, shared out equally. In our made-up example, a page with 4 links gives each one a quarter of its vote.

media.alt: A page with four arrows leaving it, each labelled with a quarter.

panels.caption: Pages that get votes from high-scoring pages score higher, and then pass on more. The paper says you can find the scores with a simple repeating calculation. Do it again and the votes shift again.

media.alt: Two circular arrows around a small group of pages.

panels.caption: The paper pictures a random surfer who keeps clicking links and sometimes gets bored and jumps to a random page. A setting called the damping factor, d, is usually set to 0.85.

media.alt: A tiny surfer clicks from page to page, then jumps to a faraway page.

strips.title: The librarian who walks the web
strips.grownUpWords: URLserver, web crawlers, storeserver and repository

panels.caption: A web crawler is like a librarian who walks the web and brings back a copy of each page. A helper called the URLserver hands out the list of addresses to visit.

media.alt: A librarian holding a list of web addresses.

panels.caption: Google usually ran about 3 crawlers, each keeping around 300 connections open at once. At its fastest, the paper says it fetched over 100 pages a second with four crawlers.

media.alt: Three librarians each holding many threads that lead to different web pages.

panels.caption: A storeserver squeezes each page smaller and files it in the repository with an ID number, a docID. The repository keeps the full page.

media.alt: A page is squeezed, given a number tag, and placed on a shelf.

strips.title: A book index for the whole web
strips.kicker: How words are looked up fast
strips.grownUpWords: hits, the forward index and the inverted index

panels.caption: The indexer reads each stored page and writes down every word with where it appeared, roughly how big the letters were, and whether it was capitalized. The paper calls each note a hit.

media.alt: A page with highlighted words and small notes beside each.

panels.caption: Then the sorter flips the lists. Instead of “this page has these words,” we get “this word is on these pages.” It is like the index at the back of a book. The paper calls it the inverted index.

media.alt: A table flipping over, turning page-to-words into word-to-pages.

panels.caption: Hit lists take up most of the space, so each hit is packed into just two bytes. Words in a title, a web address or in link text get special treatment.

media.alt: A tiny two-box package labelled hit.

strips.title: Answering one search
strips.kicker: What happens after you press Enter
strips.grownUpWords: query evaluation, doclists and the IR score combined with PageRank

panels.caption: You type “bill clinton.” The searcher turns each word into an ID number and looks up each word's list of pages in the inverted index.

media.alt: A search box with two words and two page lists coming out.

panels.caption: It scans the lists for pages that have all your words. Each match gets a score from where the words appear (title, link text, large letters, close together) combined with the page's PageRank.

media.alt: Three pages each with a score bar made of two parts.

panels.caption: The best-scoring pages are shown first. In the paper, most searches took 1 to 10 seconds, mostly waiting on disks. Repeating “al gore” took just 0.06 seconds once data was cached.

media.alt: A ranked results list with a stopwatch beside it.
